title: Class 1: Build your talking robot

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Build a Robot Desk Assistant (4 evenings)
series.summary: Four Tuesday evenings, one robot, with a study hall before each one for catching up and asking questions. Evening 1: build a robot that talks in a Deepgram voice and moves its mouth, powered by your laptop, and write its personality. Evening 2: give the servos their own power, add moving eyes, and give it several personalities you switch between by voice. Evening 3: skills (function calls) and cutting the cord: drive it from your phone over Bluetooth, or move it onto a Raspberry Pi. Evening 4: show and tell. No coding needed.

summary: Build a desk robot that talks, with a mouth that moves when it speaks. It runs on your laptop's power: three wires, no breadboard. Most of the evening goes into its personality and its Deepgram voice, and it ends with a short talk on your power options, so you know what to bring next week.
detail: Bring your own Raspberry Pi Pico W with the pins already attached; we load the robot program onto it when you check in. Your robot's body arrives already folded with its servo glued in. You draw its face, hook up the paperclip that opens its mouth, and connect the servo's three wires straight to the Pico, so your laptop powers everything. If your robot restarts every time the mouth moves, your laptop can't supply enough power: a helper gives you a breadboard, a USB power lead and a charger, and your robot gets two plugs. Then the rest of the evening happens on this page: meet Jervis, the snarky starter personality, write your own, try Deepgram voices and tune how Flux decides you've finished talking. We finish with what each wire does and your power options for Evening 2.
outcome: A robot on your table that holds a real conversation in a voice and personality you wrote, moves its mouth as it speaks, and a clip of it to share. You also know which power upgrade you want for Evening 2.
artifact: A talking desk robot running the attendee's own Deepgram voice agent, and a short video of it.
prereqs: A laptop with Google Chrome. This matters: Safari and Firefox can't talk to USB devices, so the robot won't connect in them.

Your own Raspberry Pi Pico W WITH THE PINS ALREADY ATTACHED (about $7). Look for "Pico WH" or "Pico W with headers". A Pico 2 W with headers works too. It has to be a W: the W has the radio for Bluetooth in Evening 3. A plain Pico W has no pins, so the wires can't attach without soldering.
A free Deepgram account and API key. Use the sign-up QR code at your table.
A USB port on your laptop. USB-C only laptop? We have USB-C to micro-USB cables.
Everything else is on the table.

slides.title: Build your talking robot
bullets: A desk robot that talks, and its mouth moves when it does.
About 20 minutes building, then most of the evening making it talk with Deepgram.
We finish with what powers what, so you can pick your upgrade for next week.
No coding.
slides.note: Hold up a finished robot and have it say hello. That's the whole pitch. Keep the build moving: the voice studio is the main event.

slides.title: What each robot needs
bullets: ☐ 1 × robot body, already built: folded, mouth flap hinged, tab glued in, servo glued down
☐ 1 × your own Raspberry Pi Pico W with pins (Pico WH, or Pico 2 W with headers), loaded with the robot program at check-in
☐ 3 × male-to-female jumper wires (orange signal, red power, brown ground)
☐ 1 × micro-USB data cable (not charge-only), USB-C or USB-A to match your laptop
☐ 1 × jumbo paperclip
☐ Tape and a marker
Only if your robot keeps restarting (helper table): ☐ half-size breadboard ☐ USB-to-2-pin power lead ☐ 3 × male-to-male jumpers ☐ a USB charger with the flat USB-A port
Bring: your Pico W with pins, a laptop with Google Chrome, and your Deepgram key
slides.note: Before class, helpers build every body (about 5 minutes each, so batch them the day before): fold the 8×8×8 inch box, tape the bottom shut, cut off the two front side flaps, glue the top front flap shut, glue a cut-off flap piece inside the bottom flap as a tab, and hot-glue an MG90S servo to the floor near the front with its horn on and facing up. Attendees bring their own Picos, and they arrive blank, so run a loading station at check-in (2–3 laptops, about 2 minutes a board). For each Pico: hold BOOTSEL, plug it in, and drag on the MicroPython .uf2 that matches the board (Pico W / WH: the RP2040 "Pico W" build; Pico 2 W: the RP2350 "Pico 2 W" build). When it reboots, copy the robot program on with `mpremote cp main.py :main.py`. It already has the eyes and Bluetooth, so nobody reloads it later. It prints its Bluetooth name (BLUETOOTH NAME Robot-XXXX) when it starts: write that on a sticker on the box. Test it with Connect robot, then stick a dot on it so you know it's done. Turn away no one: a Pico with no pins, or no Pico at all, gets a spare from the helper table. Helper table: breadboard kits for robots that keep resetting (breadboard, 2-pin lead, 3 male-to-male jumpers), USB-A chargers and a power strip, spare built bodies, spare data cables (the one people forget), USB-C adapters, 8–10 spare Pico WH boards, extra paperclips, one glue gun for fixes.

slides.title: Five parts, five jobs
bullets: Brain: your laptop. It hears you, talks to Deepgram and speaks.
Controller: the Pico W. It turns the page's commands into servo signals.
Actuator: the servo. It moves the mouth.
Power: 5 volts from somewhere. Tonight, the laptop's USB port.
Keep two questions apart: where the thinking happens, and where the power comes from.
slides.note: One minute. This picture comes back at the end of the evening and in Evening 3, when the brain moves off the laptop.

slides.title: Finish your robot
bullets: Put a strip of tape across the top flap and draw its eyes. (Moving eyes are an upgrade in Class 2.)
Bend the paperclip into an L.
Hook one end through a hole in the servo horn, and push the other end through the tab inside the mouth.
Turn the horn gently by hand: the mouth should open and shut.
slides.note: Done when: turning the horn by hand opens and closes the mouth. If it binds, bend the paperclip, don't force the servo.

slides.title: Every servo has 3 wires
bullets: Orange = signal. A pulse 50 times a second; how long each pulse lasts sets the angle.
Red = power. Brings in 5 volts.
Brown = ground. The way back. Every part shares one ground.
Loose orange: it never moves. Loose red or brown: nothing moves at all.
slides.note: Hold the Pico with the USB port at the top and the Raspberry Pi logo facing you. Pin 1 is top left.

slides.title: Wire it up: three wires, no breadboard
bullets: Orange → GP15 (pin 20, bottom left with the USB at the top).
Red → VBUS (pin 40, top right). That's the laptop's 5 volts.
Brown → GND (pin 38, two below VBUS).
Use the three male-to-female jumpers. Then plug the Pico into your laptop.
slides.note: The laptop feeds the Pico through the USB cable, and the Pico passes that power on to the servo through VBUS. A laptop port gives about 0.5 A; the Pico and one mouth servo use about 0.4 A, so it usually works, with no headroom. Helpers check every board before anyone plugs in: orange on pin 20, red on pin 40, brown on pin 38. Aim to have every robot plugged in by minute 20.

slides.title: Does your robot restart when the mouth moves?
bullets: That's a reset, not a short. The servo wants more power than your laptop's port gives, the Pico's voltage dips, and it restarts.
The fix: give the servo its own power. Grab a breadboard kit from the helper table.
Lead's red pin → + row, black pin → − row. Plug the lead into a USB charger.
Move the servo's red to the + row and brown to the − row. One jumper from the − row to GND (pin 23).
Take the red off pin 40: nothing on pin 40 now. Orange stays on GP15.
Now your robot has two plugs: the laptop (the brain) and the charger (the muscles).
slides.note: Plan for a lot of the room to need this: through a USB-C to micro-USB cable many laptops, new ones included, only offer about 0.5 A, and the servo spikes to about 0.7 A every time it starts moving. Dana's own laptop reset. The page reconnects by itself after a reset, but the mouth keeps stuttering until the servo has its own power. The rule: the servo's red goes to pin 40 OR the + row, never both.

slides.title: Meet the Deepgram Voice Agent
bullets: Flux listens, and works out when you've finished talking.
A language model thinks, using the personality you write.
Deepgram speaks, in the voice you choose.
One live connection does all three, in real time.
Your page turns the loudness of its voice into mouth movement.
slides.note: Two minutes, no more. Point at the How the pieces fit diagram further down the page.

slides.title: First words
bullets: Paste your Deepgram key.
Quit Thonny if it's open, then press Connect robot.
Set the mouth, slowly and in order: shut first, then open. Stop before it buzzes.
Press Wiggle the mouth to check.
Press Start talking and say hello to Jervis.
slides.note: The sliders move the servo live. Fast drags or pushing past the end of the mouth make it buzz and strain. Jervis is the starter personality: furry, snarky and a little passive-aggressive. Let people enjoy it before they change it.

slides.title: Write its personality
bullets: Press Stop. Under Personality, write who it is: its name, its job, what it cares about.
Then how it talks: short or chatty, formal or slangy, any catchphrase.
Then the rules: one or two sentences per reply, what it won't talk about, how it handles being interrupted.
Give it a Robot name and change the First thing it says.
Start again. Try to throw it off: does it stay in character?
Rewrite, test, rewrite. Most good robots take three tries.
slides.note: This is the biggest block of the evening on purpose. Ideas to offer: a grumpy pirate, a nervous first-day intern, an over-excited tour guide for The Hub, a robot that's sure it's a fridge. Point people at Jervis's prompt as an example of a full personality. One is enough tonight: in Evening 2 everyone builds more and switches between them by voice.

slides.title: Find its voice
bullets: Try three different voices, one at a time.
Same personality, different voice: which one fits?
Listen for pace, warmth, and how it says your name.
slides.note: All of these are Deepgram voices, generated live as it talks.

slides.title: Turn-taking with Flux
bullets: Set Patience to 0.5. Pause halfway through a sentence. Does it jump in?
Set it to 0.9 and try again. Notice the wait before it answers.
Flux listens for when you're done talking, not just for silence.
Try interrupting it mid-sentence: barge-in lets you cut in, like with a person.
slides.note: This is the part people remember: turn-taking is what makes a voice agent feel human or robotic. If a robot keeps stopping itself, it's hearing its own voice: switch off barge-in for that one.

slides.title: Show it off
bullets: Try to make it laugh.
Ask it something its personality would hate.
Film a 20-second clip with Film a clip and share it with #RobotLunchLab.
slides.note: Set up one well-lit corner with a plain background for filming.

slides.title: The power budget
bullets: Every 5 V source can supply only so much current. Every part draws some.
Laptop port: about 0.5 A. One USB charger port: about 2.4 A. BreadVolt: 1.5 A.
A moving servo draws about 0.3 A, with start-up spikes up to about 0.7 A.
Draw more than the source supplies and the voltage sags: the Pico browns out and resets.
slides.note: Five minutes for this whole power section. It's the why behind the resets some people hit tonight, and it sets up the choice for Evening 2.

slides.title: How many servos can each one feed?
bullets: Laptop: just the mouth.
BreadVolt battery: the mouth and two eyes.
A USB charger port: up to about five servos.
Three or more servos: add a 470–1000 µF capacitor across + and − to absorb the spikes.

slides.title: Your robot works. What next?
bullets: Want more servos (eyes, eyebrows, a neck)? That's a power upgrade: a BreadVolt, or a breadboard and a phone charger. The laptop stays the brain.
Want no laptop? That's a brain upgrade: your phone over Bluetooth, or a Raspberry Pi.
A Pi is a new brain, not more power. You don't need one to add servos.

slides.title: Your power options
bullets: Laptop only: what you have tonight. One servo, may reset.
Breadboard + phone charger: up to about 5 servos. Two plugs: laptop and wall. About $5.
Breadboard + BreadVolt: about 3 servos on a rechargeable battery. About $10.
Bluetooth: your phone becomes the brain, the robot sits on a charger or BreadVolt. About $0–20.
Raspberry Pi: a new brain inside the robot. About $130–170.
slides.note: Ask people to decide tonight what they'll bring to Evening 2. Study hall before each evening is the place to ask buying questions.

slides.title: Evening 2: more servos, more personalities
bullets: Your servos get their own power, and your robot gets moving eyes.
Bring a USB charger with the flat USB-A port (an old phone charger is perfect), or a BreadVolt (about $10) if you want it on a battery.
Moving eyes are 2 more servos. We're placing one bulk order for the group: chip in about $5 before you leave and yours arrive in time.
Robots can stay on the shelf at The Hub between evenings.
slides.note: Eye servos are a group buy, not in the budget. Collect about $5 a person at the helper table and write down every name. Right after class, Dana orders MG90S servos on Amazon for everyone who chipped in (2 each, about 100 for a full room; 12-packs work out to about $2.50 a servo) and checks the delivery date lands before Evening 2. Dana brings the eyeballs. Many new chargers are USB-C only and the 2-pin lead is USB-A: we have USB-C to USB-A adapters, but tell people to look for the flat port.

Your robot's voice studio

flow.title: Test corner, your power options and next evening

troubleshooting: Your Pico has no pins (a plain Pico W or Pico 2 W): the jumper wires can't attach without soldering. Swap it for a spare with headers from the helper table.

Connect robot shows "No compatible devices found": the Pico isn't running MicroPython and the robot program yet, it's in BOOTSEL mode (a drive called RPI-RP2 or RP2350 is open), or the cable only charges. Swap the cable first.
It says the board did not answer: the Pico isn't running the robot program. Unplug it, plug it back in and connect again. If that fails, a helper swaps the Pico.

The robot restarts (the page says it reset) every time the mouth moves: your laptop can't power the servo. Get a breadboard kit from the helper table and follow "Does your robot restart when the mouth moves?": the servo moves to a charger, and nothing stays on pin 40.
Nothing moves at all: check red is on pin 40 and brown on pin 38 (or, with a breadboard, on the + and − rows, with the lead in a charger and the ground jumper on pin 23).
The servo buzzes or twitches fast at one end: shut or open is pushing past where the mouth can go. Move it back 2 or 3 steps with the − and + buttons.
The mouth moves the wrong way: swap the shut and open numbers.
The servo twitches on its own with a breadboard: the ground jumper from the − row to pin 23 is missing.
No sound: turn up the laptop volume and check the output device in system settings.
Connect robot does nothing at all: you're not in Chrome. Open the page in Chrome (or Chromium on a Raspberry Pi).
Another program is using the port: quit Thonny and close other tabs with this page, unplug the Pico, plug it back in, and connect again.
It cuts you off: raise Patience. It's slow to answer: lower it.
It talks to itself, or stops mid-sentence for no reason: it's hearing its own voice. Switch off Let me interrupt it (barge-in), or move the laptop away from the robot's speaker.
Deepgram stopped the session: check the key was pasted whole, and that the account has credit.
